sources.provenance: MIT Civil and Environmental Engineering Communication Lab; page credits Communication Fellow Andrew Feldman for the most recent revision.
sources.read_scope: Complete substantive guide, especially Criteria for Success, Identify Your Purpose, Analyze Your Audience and Skills: The title is attractive / The abstract is key / Each paragraph starts with the message.

passages.short_quote: A great option for your title is a shortened version of your one-to-two sentence main message.
passages.paraphrase: A title can condense the main message while using accessible topic keywords; readership determines background and detail.
passages.agent_application: Compare title candidates with the evidence-supported central message and search terms.
passages.boundary: A useful option, not a mandate to use a declarative title or exactly one sentence. No title grammar/collocation list is supplied; that check remains an editorial inference.

sources.title: Journal Article: Abstract
sources.provenance: Broad Research Communication Lab on the MIT domain; page states adaptation from MIT Biological Engineering Communication Lab.
sources.read_scope: Complete substantive guide: When to Write the Abstract, Purpose and Abstract Formula; linked annotated PDFs not read.

passages.paraphrase: Distill the actual completed sections and subtract/consolidate findings until the crucial results remain.
passages.agent_application: Draft from the current Results/Discussion; rank possible quantitative anchors by what conclusion each establishes.
passages.boundary: Writing last is a tactic, not an exclusive sequence; a working abstract can guide earlier work.

passages.short_quote: Describe how your findings influence our understanding of the relevant field
passages.paraphrase: Context, question, approach, selected findings and implications jointly make the abstract informative.
passages.agent_application: End on the concrete understanding or decision changed by the finding, including a useful negative finding.
passages.boundary: The six-component formula and suggested sentence ranges are this teaching model; do not impose six sentences or a fixed number of numerical results.

sources.title: Journal Article: Introduction
sources.provenance: Broad Research Communication Lab on the MIT domain; adapted from MIT Biological Engineering Communication Lab.
sources.read_scope: Complete substantive guide: When to Write the Introduction, Purpose and Introduction Formula; annotated example PDFs not read.

passages.short_quote: Your purpose is not to showcase the breadth of your knowledge
passages.paraphrase: Supply the knowledge needed to understand the system, question and significance, then articulate a question made logical by that background.
passages.agent_application: Synthesize related evidence by what it establishes; remove background that does not help derive the current question.
passages.boundary: The four ordered components are a rhetorical model, not four paragraphs or a required broad-opening sentence.

sources.title: Journal Article: Methods
sources.provenance: Broad Research Communication Lab on the MIT domain; adapted from MIT Biological Engineering Communication Lab.
sources.read_scope: Complete substantive guide: Criteria, Identify Your Purpose, Analyze your audience, all Skills subsections; linked example PDF not read.

passages.short_quote: specify any methodological details that might cause someone to reach a different conclusion.
passages.paraphrase: Methods serve validity assessment and replication; describe purpose/application, original standard-method sources and modifications, with a logical correspondence to Results.
passages.agent_application: Preserve controls, operators, calibration data, parameter roles and changes affecting interpretation; allocate routine execution detail to an accessible reproduction record.
passages.boundary: Minimal means sufficient, not short by quota. Its avoid-we/passive preference is local advice, not universal journal policy; conflicts with UNC active-voice option are retained.

passages.short_quote: this is far from fixed or rigid, and not all the elements are present in all introductions.
passages.paraphrase: Introduction moves include context, a problem/niche and research purpose, but their presence/order varies. Phrase lists realize functions rather than supply evidence.
passages.agent_application: Use rhetorical functions to diagnose missing reasoning, then write study-specific language from verified sources.
passages.boundary: Do not paste no/few-studies phrases without a literature search. CARS here is institutional explanation of Swales, not a fresh reading of his original monograph.

sources.title: Academic Phrasebank: Describing methods
sources.provenance: University of Manchester Academic Phrasebank institutional original page.
sources.read_scope: Overview; complete categories current methodology, reasons adopted/rejected, established methods, selection/inclusion, infinitive purpose, statistical procedures and methodological problems/limitations.

passages.short_quote: clear and detailed enough for another experienced person to repeat the research and reproduce the results.
passages.paraphrase: Detail depends on method novelty, controversy and reader expertise; method descriptions include purpose, selection rules and reasons, not only actions.
passages.agent_application: Describe why the design answers the scientific question and specify exclusions/selection factually where they alter inference.
passages.boundary: The simple-past observation applies to most example functional categories, not equations, definitions or all Methods sentences. Listed statistical phrases do not license unperformed tests.

sources.title: Academic Phrasebank: Signalling transition
sources.provenance: University of Manchester Academic Phrasebank institutional original page.

passages.short_quote: It must be accurate, but it must be easy to follow.
passages.paraphrase: A preview or transition helps readers track movement between topics and sections; functions include contrast, return and summary.
passages.agent_application: Select signposting only after identifying the actual relation between adjacent argument units.
passages.boundary: Thesis-style roadmaps and repeated section summaries are available options, not a requirement for every research-article paragraph.

sources.title: Paragraphs
sources.provenance: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Writing Center, College of Arts and Sciences.
sources.read_scope: Complete substantive handout: definition, thesis/control, organization options, five-step illustration, all troubleshooting sections and reuse footer.

passages.short_quote: Length and appearance do not determine whether a section in a paper is a paragraph.
passages.paraphrase: Unity/coherence around a controlling idea, adequate evidence and explanation define a paragraph; completion can be a conclusion or transition.
passages.agent_application: Reverse-outline each paragraph by its inference and supporting evidence, then remove or relocate unrelated claims.
passages.boundary: The five-step illustration is an example, not five sentences; the topic sentence can occur later; do not force every paragraph to end with a gap or summary.

sources.title: Transitions
sources.provenance: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Writing Center, College of Arts and Sciences.
sources.read_scope: Complete substantive handout: logical function, diagnosis, organization/reverse outline, mechanics, transition types and relation table, footer.

passages.short_quote: Transitions cannot substitute for good organization
passages.paraphrase: Transitions expose relations already built into the argument. Diagnose organization before adding however/therefore or roadmaps.
passages.agent_application: Write the relation in plain words; if no relation can be named, reorder or repair the reasoning first.
passages.boundary: Connectors can introduce unjustified causal/contrast claims. There is no requirement to insert a connector in every paragraph.

sources.title: Scientific Writing
sources.provenance: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Writing Center, College of Arts and Sciences.
sources.read_scope: Complete substantive handout: precision, word choice, detail, quantification, clarity, sentence structure, verbosity, objectivity/voice and limitations; footer.

passages.paraphrase: Choose terms for their precise scientific meaning, keep subjects and actions legible, include necessary details and avoid unsupported generalization.
passages.agent_application: Check title noun relationships and collocations against their intended physical meaning; keep stable terms rather than decorative synonyms.
passages.boundary: Its sentence/preposition rules are heuristics, not automatic thresholds. Objective claims depend on evidence and scope, not passive voice.

passages.short_quote: Currently, the active voice is preferred in most scientific fields
passages.paraphrase: Active voice can be clear and acceptable; editorial preferences vary. Passive can be useful but may become awkward.
passages.agent_application: Choose the grammatical subject to clarify the scientific action; never invent what an author did, and do not equate we with subjectivity.
passages.boundary: This statement is writing-center advice, not a verified present-day survey of every journal; check the actual target requirement.

sources.title: Ten simple rules for structuring papers
sources.provenance: Brett Mensh and Konrad Kording, PLOS Computational Biology 13(9):e1005619 (2017); publisher original scholarly advice article; DOI10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005619.
sources.read_scope: Overview, Introduction, full Rules1–10 and Discussion; relevant Figure1/Table1 captions in text; image pixels not inspected; linked correction not substantively read.

passages.short_quote: make the claim and/or model as simple as the data and logic can support but no simpler.
passages.paraphrase: A central contribution focuses title and whole paper; complexity should follow evidence, and one contribution can be multifaceted.
passages.agent_application: Write a contribution sentence and trace it to comparisons, figures and limits before revising prose.
passages.boundary: Central contribution need not be improved accuracy or a new algorithm. This advice is not the target journal author guide.

passages.short_quote: Every scientific argument has its own particular logical structure
passages.paraphrase: Results form a sequence of evidence-supported statements, not a chronology of work; negative/hypothesis-disproving findings can advance the argument.
passages.agent_application: Select result units by what question they answer and connect them to the central contribution.
passages.boundary: CCC and gap-ending paragraphs are advocated defaults, not universal paragraph templates. No fixed title/abstract numbers or paragraph counts follow.

sources.provenance: University of Southern California Libraries Research Guide. Institutional authored/curated teaching page, drawing on cited writing literature; not those cited originals themselves.

passages.short_quote: Indicate accurately the subject and scope of the study
passages.paraphrase: Titles should identify the research focus/scope and use current field nomenclature; subtitles can qualify context or method.
passages.agent_application: Test each modifier and relational phrase for a supported meaning; distinguish topic, relationship and scope before removing words.
passages.boundary: The 5–12 substantive-word suggestion, capitalization and social-science examples are conventions of this guide, not universal requirements. Its flexible title-form advice does not excuse ambiguity or unsupported causality.
